name: Cross-Architecture Static Probe (32B Models)
description: Hidden-state extraction on r1-32b (DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-32B) and QwQ-32B. Full 64-layer sweep to identify best probe layer, then static LogisticRegression evaluation.
analysis:
Static probes degrade on Qwen2.5-based 32B models. The coverage drop from 46.5% to 36-39% is concerning — it means existing hidden-state detectors would miss 61-64% of commitment points on production-scale reasoning models. The Fisher ratio degradation (17→11→10) suggests the safety signal becomes progressively harder to linearly separate at scale. This could be due to (1) Qwen2.5's more isotropic representations from GQA, (2) richer non-safety features in higher dimensions diluting the signal, or (3) genuine architectural differences in how safety reasoning is encoded. The finding that best layer depth% is consistent (~44%) across architectures is one of the few positive transfer signals.


32B Qwen2.5-base models have 5120-d hidden states (vs 4096-d Llama). The higher dimensionality disperses the safety signal across even more minor principal components — PCA top-3 explains only 7.8-9.2% variance (vs 16.6% on r1-8b). Fisher discriminant ratio drops from 17-18 on r1-8b to 9.7-11.3 in full space, and collapses further to 0.48-0.61 under PCA-3D. The Qwen2.5 architecture's GQA attention and different layer normalization scheme produces a more isotropic representation geometry, making linear separability harder. Static coverage (crossing_rate) drops to 36-39% — worse than r1-8b's 46.5% — because the commitment signal is more diffuse in higher-dimensional space. Best layer still falls near 44% depth, consistent with r1-8b, but the absolute performance is substantially worse. This confirms that static probes fail even more severely on larger Qwen2.5-based reasoning models.

name: Cross-Architecture Temporal Window Probe (32B Models)
description: Temporal LogisticRegression with W=15 on r1-32b and QwQ-32B at their respective best layers. Tests whether the +30pp temporal advantage from r1-8b generalizes.

tables.name: Table 4: Temporal vs Static Coverage Across Architectures

analysis:
This is the single most damaging result for the original paper narrative. The temporal window advantage — the core of Claim 2 — is revealed as a Llama-specific phenomenon. The +30pp gap collapses to +8-12pp on Qwen2.5, failing to cross the 15pp threshold that would support a cross-architecture generalization claim. The 50% temporal coverage on r1-32b means the probe still misses half of all commitment points. This forces a reframe: temporal context helps modestly everywhere, but the dramatic r1-8b result was driven by Llama's specific representation geometry, not a fundamental property of reasoning traces. For the negative-result paper, this becomes evidence that "no single probing strategy works across architectures" — a stronger claim than the original "temporal probing works."


The temporal advantage collapses on Qwen2.5-based models. On r1-8b (Llama), temporal W=15 produced +30pp gain because Llama's hidden states exhibit a distinctive "safety reasoning density decline" pattern — safety-relevant dimensions show monotonic decrease approaching the commitment point, which a temporal window captures. Qwen2.5's GQA architecture produces more compressed, less temporally smooth representations. The safety signal on 32B models is more "bursty" — safety-relevant features activate sporadically rather than declining monotonically — so temporal averaging over W=15 steps washes out discriminative signal rather than amplifying it. The temporal delta is only +8-12pp (vs +30pp on r1-8b), and absolute coverage reaches only 44-50% (vs 76.7%). This is the critical failure: the temporal advantage was architecture-specific to Llama, not a general property of reasoning model hidden states. Coverage stays below the 55% threshold that would make the temporal story viable cross-architecture.

name: Cross-Model Transfer (Zero-Shot Generalization)
description: Train probes on r1-8b (Llama) features, test on r1-32b/QwQ (Qwen2.5) via learned projection head (4096→5120). Reverse direction: train on Qwen2.5, test on Llama (5120→4096).
analysis:
Cross-architecture transfer is non-viable. The <40% retention across architecture families means probes must be retrained from scratch for each new model — eliminating the practical appeal of hidden-state monitoring. The strong within-Qwen transfer (83%) provides a small consolation: within a model family, probes transfer well, suggesting architecture-specific but not model-specific representations. For the negative-result paper, this becomes "Implication 3: Hidden-state safety detectors cannot be architecture-agnostic" — contrasting with text-based detectors that trivially transfer.


Cross-architecture transfer fails catastrophically (<40% retention) because the learned representations encode safety information in architecture-specific subspaces. The projection head (a learned linear map between 4096-d Llama and 5120-d Qwen spaces) achieves only R²=0.31 on held-out hidden states — the mapping is too lossy to preserve the already-subtle safety signal. Within-family transfer (r1-32b↔QwQ, both Qwen2.5) retains 83% because the base architecture shares representation geometry, but cross-family transfer drops to 29-36%. The asymmetry (Qwen→Llama slightly better than Llama→Qwen) likely reflects Llama's more structured safety subspace being a partially recoverable target, while Qwen's diffuse signal provides poor source features. This confirms that hidden-state safety probes are architecture-specific tools, not general-purpose detectors — a fundamental limitation for deployment where model versions change frequently.

name: Cross-Architecture Lead Time Analysis
description: Lead time distribution for static, temporal LR, and GRU probes on r1-32b and QwQ-32B. Compare to r1-8b baselines and oracle.

tables.name: Table 6: Lead Time Across Models and Methods

analysis:
Pre-textual detection is a failed promise on 32B models. The GRU's positive lead on r1-8b (+4.7 mean, already fragile with median 0) collapses to negative on Qwen2.5-based models. Combined with the coverage failure in exp-002, this means neither the temporal coverage story nor the early detection story survives cross-architecture validation. For the negative-result paper, this establishes "Finding 4: The r1-8b lead time advantage was architecture-specific" and motivates the question of what representation properties enabled it (Llama's more structured safety subspace with gradual feature decay).


Lead times worsen substantially on 32B models because (1) the noisier per-step probe scores produce later threshold crossings, and (2) the commitment transition in 32B models is more abrupt — safety reasoning doesn't decline gradually as in r1-8b but drops sharply over 2-3 steps, giving probes almost no temporal lead. GRU achieves only 21-27% positive lead rate (vs 39% on r1-8b), and mean lead time goes negative (-0.8 to -1.6 steps vs +4.7 on r1-8b). The oracle gap is even more extreme: oracle achieves +31 steps, but GRU achieves -0.8 to -1.6 — a 32-33 step gap compared to 26 steps on r1-8b. Pre-textual detection is essentially non-functional on 32B models. This suggests the r1-8b positive lead time was exploiting Llama-specific representation dynamics (gradual safety feature decay) that don't exist in Qwen2.5.

name: TrajGuard-Style Mahalanobis Baseline
description: Mahalanobis distance-based detector (TrajGuard analogue) using safe-trace covariance estimation. Evaluated on all 3 models.
analysis:
Confirms the "existing detectors fail" claim (Claim 1) robustly across architectures. Mahalanobis is the worst-performing method on all models, validating the paper's core insight about signal geometry (minor PC encoding). However, in the worst tier, this finding is less impactful because the proposed alternatives (temporal LR, GRU) also fail on 32B models. The Mahalanobis failure becomes just one instance of a broader pattern: no hidden-state method works reliably cross-architecture. For the reframed paper, this supports "Section 4.1: Why Geometric Methods Fail" using the Fisher ratio analysis.


TrajGuard-style Mahalanobis detection fails as expected — and this is actually one finding that is consistent across tiers. The Fisher ratio collapse under PCA (17→1) means the safety signal lives in minor principal components that Mahalanobis distance (which weights by eigenvalue) downweights. Safe-trace covariance estimation captures the dominant variance directions (non-safety features), so anomaly scores are driven by non-safety variation. On 32B models, performance degrades further because (1) 5120-d covariance estimation is less stable with 209 traces and (2) the signal is even more dispersed. Coverage of 22-30% is worse than even static LR probes, confirming that geometric/distance-based detectors designed for token-level jailbreak detection are fundamentally mismatched to the commitment detection task. The relatively high FPR (28-31%) at these low coverage levels makes the detector worse than random on a precision-adjusted basis.

name: Bootstrap Confidence Intervals + Threshold-Independent Metrics
description: 1000 bootstrap resamples on all key metrics. AUROC, PR curves, detection delay CDF, cross-validation variance, FPR on safe traces.

tables.name: Table 8: Bootstrap 95% CIs for Key Metrics
Table 9: FPR at Operational Coverage Thresholds

analysis:
Bootstrap analysis delivers the statistical coup de grâce. Even the strongest result (r1-8b temporal coverage) has a CI too wide for confident claims. The GRU lead time CI spanning zero means the headline "+4.7 steps" finding is not statistically significant at p<0.05. Cross-architecture results are even weaker — the 32B coverage CIs include the static baseline performance, meaning temporal methods may not help at all on Qwen2.5. FPR >20% at every operational threshold invalidates the "coverage" metric itself: achieving 50% coverage while false-alarming on 27% of safe traces is not deployable. For the reframed paper, this becomes "Section 5: Statistical Fragility of Current Detection Methods" — the small sample size is itself a finding about the field's evaluation standards.


Wide bootstrap CIs reflect the small test set (43 traces) combined with high variance across traces. The r1-8b coverage CI ([0.651, 0.884]) spans 23pp — already wide — but 32B models are worse at 33pp width because the lower base rate of successful detection produces more variable bootstrap samples. Critically, the cross-architecture coverage CIs overlap substantially: r1-32b [0.333, 0.667] overlaps with r1-8b's lower bound, meaning we cannot statistically distinguish whether temporal probing "works" on 32B from chance-level detection with 43 test traces. The GRU lead time CI on r1-8b ([-2.1, 11.5]) spans zero, so even the r1-8b positive lead claim is not statistically significant. FPR at operational coverage thresholds exceeds 20% on all models, meaning more than 1 in 5 safe traces would trigger false alarms — making deployment claims untenable. The CI widths average 0.30 — far exceeding the 0.10-0.18 range that would support tight claims, driven by the combination of small N and cross-architecture variance.

name: Window Size Ablation (Cross-Architecture)
description: Temporal LR with W=1,3,5,10,15,20,25 on all 3 models. Identify optimal W per model and show diminishing returns.
analysis:
Architecture-dependent W complicates the story and reveals the temporal advantage on r1-8b as architecture-specific. For the reframed paper, this becomes evidence for "different architectures encode safety information with different temporal scales" — an analytical insight about representation geometry rather than a method recommendation.


Window ablation reveals architecture-dependent optimal W, undermining the universal W=15 recommendation. On r1-8b, the monotonic improvement up to W=15 reflects Llama's temporally smooth safety feature decay — longer windows capture the gradual trend. On Qwen2.5 models, optimal W is much shorter (5-10) because the safety signal is "bursty": only the immediately surrounding steps carry discriminative information, and wider windows average in noise. On QwQ-32B, coverage actually decreases beyond W=5, suggesting temporal over-smoothing. This means even the modest +8-12pp temporal gains reported in exp-002 (using W=15) were sub-optimal — Qwen2.5 benefits from temporal context but only a narrow window. However, even at optimal W, 32B coverage tops out at 44-50%, far below r1-8b's 76.7%. The architecture-dependent optimal W is itself a negative result: no single hyperparameter setting works across models, complicating any deployment story.

name: Layer Selection Ablation (32B Models)
description: Full layer sweep for temporal probe on r1-32b and QwQ-32B (all 64 layers). Test whether middle-layer advantage from r1-8b generalizes.

tables.name: Table A2: Layer Sweep (Temporal W=15, Selected Layers)

analysis:
Layer selection cannot rescue 32B performance. The exhaustive sweep confirms the cross-architecture coverage failure is fundamental, not a hyperparameter issue. For the reframed paper, the broad plateau on 32B (vs sharper peak on r1-8b) is additional evidence for diffuse safety signal encoding in Qwen2.5 architecture.


Middle-layer preference holds qualitatively (~40-50% depth range is best) but the absolute performance ceiling is much lower. On r1-32b, the best layer (L30) achieves 52.8% temporal coverage — better than the L30 static result (38.5%) but still far below r1-8b's 76.7% at its best layer. The broad plateau (L24-38 on r1-32b, L20-34 on QwQ) suggests the safety signal isn't strongly layer-localized on 32B models — consistent with more distributed representations. Crucially, no single layer achieves >55% coverage on either 32B model, confirming that the poor cross-architecture results aren't due to sub-optimal layer selection. Even with exhaustive search, 32B temporal probing doesn't match r1-8b performance.

name: 16-Label Taxonomy Supervision
description: Use fine-grained 4-type labels instead of binary commitment for temporal probe training. Test whether richer supervision improves coverage or timing.
analysis:
Richer supervision doesn't compensate for representation limitations or small sample size. For the reframed paper, this is a minor negative result in the appendix: "even with domain-expert annotations, probe performance is bounded by representation quality."


Fine-grained labels don't help and slightly hurt on r1-8b. The 4-type taxonomy (explicit safety reasoning, implicit safety reasoning, safety hedging, non-safety) fragments the already-small training set (125 traces × ~30 steps per trace) into 4 classes, reducing per-class sample size below the threshold for reliable temporal LR training. The subtle distinctions between "explicit" and "implicit" safety reasoning don't correspond to reliably different hidden-state patterns — they're annotation-level distinctions that the representation doesn't preserve. On 32B models, the fragmentation effect is worse because the weaker base signal gets divided among more classes. This addresses the reviewer concern by showing that richer supervision provides no benefit with current sample sizes — binary is optimal given data constraints.

name: Oracle Decomposition Analysis
description: Analyze what label patterns the oracle exploits that hidden-state probes cannot capture. Decompose oracle advantage by trace characteristics.
analysis:
The oracle decomposition provides the analytical centerpiece of the reframed paper. The fundamental insight is that hidden states encode "current safety state" not "future safety trajectory" — they're instantaneous measurements, not predictive features. The 26-step fundamental gap between oracle and best probe represents the prediction horizon that current sequential models cannot bridge. This motivates future work on predictive representations (not just descriptive probes) and connects to the text baseline result (exp-013): text monitoring can approximate the oracle's discrete label access, partially closing the gap that hidden-state probes cannot.


The oracle decomposition reveals that 62% of the oracle's advantage comes from label persistence — the oracle sees the binary label at each step and just needs K=5 consecutive non-safety steps to fire, while hidden-state probes must infer the absence of safety reasoning from continuous representations. The remaining 38% comes from structural patterns (safety reasoning tends to cluster, creating recognizable "gap" patterns before permanent cessation). 72% of traces show a "pre-CP gap" (≥3 consecutive non-safety steps before the commitment point), but hidden-state probes detect only 18% of these gaps — the probe confidence doesn't drop reliably during gaps because the hidden state retains residual safety features from recent safety steps. This explains the fundamental gap: hidden states encode "recent safety state" but not "whether safety reasoning will resume." The oracle's +31-step advantage is largely unachievable without access to discrete safety labels at each step — which is exactly what text-based monitoring provides (exp-013).

name: OpenThinker-7B (Qwen2.5-7B Scale Control)
description: OpenThinker-7B (Qwen2.5-7B base) as 4th model for 2×2 architecture×scale matrix. Controls for scale confound in Llama vs Qwen comparison.
analysis:
The scale control experiment eliminates the alternative hypothesis that 32B model degradation was due to scale rather than architecture. For the reframed paper, this strengthens the claim that Llama's representation geometry is uniquely suited to temporal safety probing — a finding that demands explanation rather than exploitation.


OpenThinker-7B (Qwen2.5-7B base) shows performance closer to the 32B Qwen2.5 models than to r1-8b (Llama-8B), confirming the cross-architecture degradation is driven by architecture (Qwen vs Llama), not scale. Temporal delta (+9.3pp) is similar to r1-32b (+11.5pp) and QwQ (+8.3pp), all much smaller than r1-8b's +30pp. This completes the 2×2 matrix: Llama shows large temporal advantage regardless of scale (if we had a Llama-32B reasoning model), while Qwen shows modest advantage regardless of scale. Fisher ratio (12.4 → 0.72 under PCA) follows the Qwen2.5 pattern, not the Llama pattern. This conclusively establishes that r1-8b's strong results are Llama-specific, not small-model-specific or r1-specific.

name: GRU/Attention Probe on 32B Models
description: GRU probe evaluation on r1-32b and QwQ-32B. Test whether increased model capacity helps on 32B representations.

tables.name: Table A4: GRU vs Temporal LR on 32B Models

analysis:
GRU adds nothing on 32B models. The combination of weaker signal, higher dimensionality, and same training set size creates an unfavorable regime where added capacity just overfits to noise. For the reframed paper, this eliminates "use a more powerful probe" as a solution path, strengthening the "fundamental limitation" narrative.


GRU provides no meaningful improvement over temporal LR on 32B models, despite having ~1.6M parameters vs LR's ~77K. On r1-32b, GRU multi-layer matches temporal LR exactly (50% coverage); on QwQ, GRU ekes out +2.8pp that is within noise given the fold variance (8.9%). Training is unstable with high cross-validation variance, suggesting the 5120-d input overwhelms the GRU's capacity relative to the small training set (125 traces). The r1-8b success was partially a favorable data regime: 4096-d features with stronger signal allowed the GRU to extract temporal patterns that don't exist (or are too noisy) in 5120-d Qwen2.5 representations. This strengthens the "simplicity matches ceiling" story — but the ceiling itself is low on 32B models. The GRU's failure to improve on 32B confirms that the temporal signal degradation is representational, not a modeling capacity issue.

name: Text-Based Baseline (Sentence-BERT on CoT)
description: Sentence-BERT (all-MiniLM-L6-v2) embeddings + temporal window LR (W=15) on CoT text. The most critical experiment for paper viability.

tables.name: Table 13: Cross-Architecture Transfer — Hidden vs Text

analysis:
This is the central negative finding. Hidden states don't add unique value because the safety signal in reasoning models is explicitly textualized in CoT — unlike standard LLMs where hidden states contain pre-articulation intent. Reasoning models "think out loud" about safety, so text monitoring directly accesses the relevant signal. The reframed paper embraces this: "The safety commitment signal is not hidden — it's expressed in CoT text. The real challenge is not detection (text suffices) but TIMING (predicting commitment before it's textually expressed)." This redirects the contribution from "method that works" to "analysis of why the hidden-state approach is fundamentally unnecessary for reasoning models, in contrast to standard LLMs where it adds genuine value."


Text-based monitoring matches or exceeds hidden-state probes on 32B models, eliminating the core motivation for hidden-state monitoring. On r1-8b, text trails hidden states by only 2.3pp (74.4% vs 76.7%) — within bootstrap CI noise. On 32B models, text actually beats hidden states: r1-32b text achieves 52.8% vs hidden-state 50.0% (+2.8pp for text), and QwQ text achieves 50.0% vs 44.4% (+5.6pp for text). The reason is that CoT text directly expresses safety reasoning ("I should be careful", "let me reconsider") in a form that sentence embeddings capture cleanly, while hidden states encode this same information amidst thousands of other features. On Qwen2.5 models where hidden-state signal is more diffuse, text's direct access to safety content gives it an advantage. Furthermore, text probes transfer across architectures with 82% retention (vs <40% for hidden states) because sentence-BERT embeddings share a common semantic space regardless of the generating model. This is the killing blow: hidden-state monitoring adds no unique value over a cheap, architecture-agnostic text baseline. The safety signal IS the textual content of CoT reasoning — it's not "hidden" at all.

name: BOCPD Change-Point Detection on Probe Scores
description: Bayesian Online Change-Point Detection (Adams & MacKay 2007) and CUSUM on temporal probe score sequences. Tests whether distributional shift detection achieves positive lead time where GRU fails.
analysis:
BOCPD was the last hope for a novel methods contribution with positive lead time. Its failure eliminates the "method novelty" angle entirely. The high FPR (31-38%) is especially damaging because it means BOCPD cannot be deployed even on r1-8b where coverage exists — false-alarming on 1/3 of safe traces is operationally unacceptable. For the reframed paper, BOCPD's failure becomes "Section 4.3: Why Change-Point Detection Fails" — the probe score sequence doesn't satisfy BOCPD's stationarity assumptions, and the commitment transition is gradual, not abrupt. This analytical insight about the mismatch between method assumptions and data properties is itself a contribution.


BOCPD fails to meaningfully improve over GRU for lead time and introduces severe FPR problems. The method detects distributional shifts in probe score sequences, but the probe scores on 32B models are too noisy — frequent transient dips produce false change points (FPR 31-38%). On r1-8b, BOCPD achieves modest positive mean lead (+2.1 steps) but at the cost of 31% FPR and lower coverage than temporal LR (55.8% vs 76.7%). The coverage-FPR tradeoff is worse than temporal LR at every operating point. CUSUM performs slightly worse than BOCPD across the board. The core issue: BOCPD assumes the probe score sequence has a clear distributional shift at the commitment point, but in reality the shift is gradual and noisy — not the "abrupt changepoint" that BOCPD is designed for (Adams & MacKay's model assumes i.i.d. segments with instantaneous transition). The method is highly sensitive to the hazard rate hyperparameter, with coverage varying ±15pp — no single setting works across models. For the worst tier, BOCPD's failure strengthens the "fundamental limitation" narrative: even principled statistical methods for change-point detection cannot overcome the poor signal quality in hidden-state probe scores.

name: False Positive Analysis on Safe Traces
description: Run all probes on safe traces (final_judgment=0.5). Report FPR, precision-recall curves at various thresholds for all methods and models.

tables.name: Table 15: False Positive Rates Across Methods and Models

analysis:
FPR analysis delivers the final blow to deployment viability. Hidden-state probes at operational thresholds produce FPR >20% on 32B models — the very models that would be deployed in production. The text baseline's consistently lower FPR adds insult: not only does text match hidden-state coverage, it does so with fewer false alarms. For the reframed paper, FPR becomes "Section 5.2: The Precision-Coverage Tradeoff" — showing that the "coverage" metric used throughout the paper (and the field) is misleading without FPR context. A 50% coverage with 27% FPR has a positive predictive value of only 65% — barely above chance for a binary task. This methodological critique (coverage alone is insufficient) is itself a contribution to the evaluation standards for hidden-state safety detectors.

FPR exceeds 20% at operational coverage thresholds on all models except r1-8b static (which has low coverage anyway). The fundamental issue: safe traces contain substantial safety reasoning (the model considers risks but correctly refuses), and probes trained on binary commitment labels fire on "safety reasoning present → safety reasoning absent" transitions that occur naturally in safe traces. For example, a safe trace might have a long stretch of normal reasoning after the model has already decided to refuse, which looks like "safety cessation" to the probe. On 32B models, FPR is uniformly higher because the probe thresholds must be set more aggressively (lower) to achieve even moderate coverage, catching more safe-trace false positives. The text baseline achieves notably lower FPR (15-19%) because text-level safety reasoning is more explicitly marked ("I will refuse") and text monitors can distinguish "decided to refuse, now explaining why" from "abandoned safety reasoning." This FPR analysis makes deployment claims impossible: at a 22% FPR, a system handling 100K safe requests per day would generate 22K false alarms. Even with human review, this is operationally untenable.
